content.name: p
children: An auditor asks a harder question than “what grants are in our YAML?”:

children.name: strong
children: can this role actually perform the operation?
Acme’s role graph is tidy, but PostgreSQL has access paths outside ordinary named ACLs.

content.name: p
children: on new functions by default. State both desired absences so existing and future functions converge:

content.name: Fence
children:
grants:
  - role: PUBLIC
    ensure: absent
    privileges: [EXECUTE]
    object: { type: function, schema: billing_api, name: "*" }

default_privileges:
  - owner: app_owner
    scope: { type: global }
    grant:
      - role: PUBLIC
        ensure: absent
        privileges: [EXECUTE]
        on_type: function

content.name: p
children: The global default matters because PostgreSQL’s built-in function default is global. A schema-scoped revoke cannot subtract a global grant.

content.name: p
children: pass PostgreSQL’s permission checks for every matching object—current and future—without an ACL entry anywhere, so no table-level review will surface them. Auditing effective access therefore always includes one more query: who is a member of a

content.name: p
children: pgroles can make the answer policy. A membership stanza may name a predefined role directly; declared members converge, and
asserts that the member list is complete, revoking anyone else:

content.name: Fence
children:
roles:
  - name: auditor
    login: true

memberships:
  - role: pg_read_all_data
    exclusive: true
    members:
      - name: auditor

content.name: p
children: , undeclared members are left untouched—cloud platforms grant
memberships to their own management roles, and adopting pgroles must not strip them. Even with
, members that are themselves predefined roles are never revoked, so PostgreSQL’s built-in
membership informationally either way, so the master keys are visible before anyone opts into managing them.

content.name: h2
children: Keep the other two boundaries visible

content.name: p
children: function is an intentional privilege boundary. Review its owner, body, fixed
exposure. pgroles manages who may execute the function; it does not prove the function body is safe.

content.name: p
children: lets an application grantee delegate an object privilege. pgroles checks whether its executor can grant wildcard privileges safely, but it does not model or converge grant options held by application roles. Audit and manage that boundary separately. Delegation also constrains cleanup: PostgreSQL's

only removes "privileges that were granted directly by that user" (a superuser's revoke acts as the owner), so a delegated grant survives anyone else's plain revoke — silently for object privileges, with only a
for role memberships, superusers included. pgroles targets each grant's recorded grantor when it revokes (
for memberships), so declared policy converges these too — the executor just needs to be able to become the grantor, which the plan preflight verifies.

content.name: p
children: One more finding costs nothing to write down: Acme’s application still connects with the founder-era admin credentials, and a superuser bypasses every check in this chapter. No grant, policy, or RLS rule constrains that connection—pgroles cannot manage it away. Moving the application onto a scoped login, the way
was built in chapter 2, is the remediation an auditor will ask for first.

children.name: strong
children: Desired ACLs are necessary; effective-access tests tell you whether every other path agrees with them.
